body.objective: Students will be able to greet and say goodbye.
body.iCan: I can greet and say goodbye.
successCriteria: I can greet people and say goodbye in Mandarin
I can use polite greetings for teachers and elders
I can respond to thanks and apologies
body.hook: 你好! Nǐ hǎo! These two characters are probably the most famous words in Mandarin. Today you'll learn how to greet people properly, including teachers and elders, and say goodbye.

study.title: 你好!
study.question: How do I greet people in Mandarin?
study.passage:
Dialogue (read with a partner):
学生 (student): 老师好! Lǎoshī hǎo!
老师 (teacher): 你们好! Nǐmen hǎo! (Hello, everyone!)
小明 Xiǎo Míng: 你好! Nǐ hǎo!
小红 Xiǎo Hóng: 你好! 你好吗? Nǐ hǎo! Nǐ hǎo ma? (How are you?)
小明: 我很好, 谢谢。你呢? Wǒ hěn hǎo, xièxie. Nǐ ne? (I'm fine, thanks. And you?)
小红: 我也很好。再见! Wǒ yě hěn hǎo. Zàijiàn! (I'm fine too. Bye!)
小明: 再见! Zàijiàn!
Culture: 您 nín is the respectful "you," used with teachers, elders and strangers. In China, students often stand and greet the teacher together at the start of class: 老师好! Friends often greet with questions like 你吃了吗? Nǐ chī le ma? (Have you eaten?), a friendly way of showing care.
Activity: role-play greetings in three situations: a friend, a teacher in the morning, a grandparent. Choose 你 or 您.
study.source: Original dialogue written for this lesson.
steps: Read the dialogue in pinyin and characters
discussion: When do you use 您 instead of 你?
How do you answer 你好吗?
What does 你吃了吗 show about culture?
How do students greet teachers in China?
study.product: Perform three greeting role-plays (friend, teacher, elder), choosing 你 or 您 correctly, and include thanks and goodbye.

practice.q: How do you say thank you?

body.objective: Students will be able to introduce my name and age.
body.iCan: I can introduce my name and age.
successCriteria: I can say my name with 我叫 and 我姓
I can say my age with 岁
I can ask someone's name, age and nationality
body.hook: 我叫… wǒ jiào… In just a few words you can tell someone your name, age and nationality. You'll also discover how Chinese names work, family name first.

study.title: 我叫…
study.question: How do I introduce myself in Mandarin?
study.passage:
Dialogue (read with a partner):
A: 你好! 你叫什么名字? Nǐ hǎo! Nǐ jiào shénme míngzi? (What's your name?)
B: 我叫王丽。你呢? Wǒ jiào Wáng Lì. Nǐ ne?
A: 我叫 Sam。你姓王吗? Wǒ jiào Sam. Nǐ xìng Wáng ma? (Is your family name Wang?)
B: 对, 我姓王。你几岁? Duì, wǒ xìng Wáng. Nǐ jǐ suì? (How old are you?)
A: 我十二岁。你是中国人吗? Wǒ shí'èr suì. Nǐ shì Zhōngguó rén ma?
B: 不是, 我是加拿大人。 Bú shì, wǒ shì Jiānádà rén.
Grammar: question particle 吗 ma turns a statement into a yes/no question: 你是加拿大人吗?
Age: no verb needed: 我十二岁 (I twelve years). For adults, 您多大年纪? is more polite.
Names: Chinese names put the family name first: 王丽 = family name 王 Wáng + given name 丽 Lì. Common family names include 王 Wáng, 李 Lǐ, 张 Zhāng, 刘 Liú and 陈 Chén.
Nationality: country + 人 rén: 中国人, 加拿大人, 美国人.
Activity: choose or receive a Chinese name, then interview three classmates.
study.source: Original dialogue written for this lesson.
discussion: What is 王丽's family name?
How do you turn a statement into a question?
Why is there no verb in 我十二岁?
What order do Chinese names use?
study.product: Write and perform a self-introduction with your name, family name, age and nationality, and ask a partner three questions.

body.objective: Students will be able to read and write basic characters.
body.iCan: I can read and write basic characters.
successCriteria: I can read and write ten basic characters
I can follow basic stroke order rules
I can explain how some characters developed from pictures
body.hook: Many Chinese characters began as pictures: 人 looks like a walking person, 山 like a mountain with three peaks, 日 was once a circle for the sun. Learning their stories makes them easier to remember.

study.title: 汉字
study.question: How are basic Chinese characters written and remembered?
study.passage:
Characters (written for this lesson):
Pictograph stories: 人 rén (person): two legs walking. 口 kǒu (mouth): an open mouth. 日 rì (sun, day): once a circle with a dot. 月 yuè (moon, month): a crescent moon. 山 shān (mountain): three peaks. 水 shuǐ (water): flowing streams. 木 mù (tree): trunk, branches and roots. 大 dà (big): a person with arms stretched wide. 小 xiǎo (small): small bits. 中 zhōng (middle): a line through the centre of a box.
Stroke order rules: 1. Top to bottom (三). 2. Left to right (川). 3. Horizontal before vertical (十). 4. Outside before inside, then close the box (日: left side, top and right, middle line, bottom). 5. Middle before sides when symmetrical (小).
Character combinations: 大人 dàrén (adult), 中国 Zhōngguó (China), 日本 Rìběn (Japan), 山水 shānshuǐ (landscape).
Activities: 1. Match characters to ancient pictures. 2. Practise each character on grid paper, counting strokes aloud. 3. Character bingo.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; character origins summarized from common teaching resources.
steps: Match them to their picture origins
discussion: Which character looks most like its meaning?
Which stroke order rule is hardest?
What does 大人 mean, and why?
study.product: Write ten characters neatly with correct stroke order on grid paper, labelled with pinyin, meaning and a picture story.

practice.a: Top to bottom; left to right.
It makes characters neat, consistent and easier to read and remember.
A person with arms stretched wide.

practice.q: Why do characters combine into words?
practice.a: To build new meanings from simpler ones.

misconceptions: Thinking every character is a picture
